newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Former Yugoslav PM urges fair elections, free media.
newsitem.headline: Former Yugoslav PM urges fair elections, free media.

text.p: A former Yugoslav prime minister urged Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Tuesday to organise free and fair elections and called for independent Serbian media.

"I challenge you to take the steps necessary to establish the conditions to ensure that the upcoming elections for the Serbian presidency and parliament will be free and fair," Milan Panic, Yugoslavia's moderate prime minister until 1992, said in a letter to Milosevic.
"The dignity of the Serbian nation can be fully restored only if all future elections pass the test of the most rigorous international scrutiny."

"The essential first step to achieve this goal is to assure that the Serbian media is fully independent and free... I call upon you to free up the media - television, radio, newspapers and periodicals - immediately," Panic said in the letter which was also faxed to Reuters.

Panic, an American millionaire of Serb origin, stood against Milosevic in the 1992 elections. Milosevic, backed by a harsh anti-Panic state media campaign, won with 55 percent of the vote against Panic's 36 percent.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) criticised the running of the elections.
In his letter Panic condemned the use of state television for party propaganda and said all candidates for public office should have universal access to the media.
Panic has not yet said if he would stand in elections due by the end of the year, but authoritative sources have said he wants to have another go at his rival Milosevic.
Milosevic's popularity plummeted to 13.5 percent in February from 32 percent last September, a survey of 2,404 people by the Mark-Plan agency showed on Tuesday.

The same survey put support for Zoran Djindjic, the new Mayor of Belgrade and co-leader of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, at 14 percent, making this the first time in Milosevic's 10-year rule that he has trailed behind another politician.
Milosevic's popularity took a beating after his ruling Socialists annulled Zajedno's local election victories in the 14 largest Serbian cities, including Belgrade, in November.
Last month Zajedno won a three-month battle to have these election victories reinstated after staging daily protests across Serbia.
But on Monday, Milosevic's Socialists unveiled a draft press law restricting privately-owned media.

The bill states that no private radio or television station would be allowed to broadcast to an audience of more than 25 percent of the 10.5 million population and that no individual could own more than 20 percent of all newsprint in Serbia.
The opposition slammed the bill and threatened more street protests unless it was amended at a televised round table discussion on free press and election rules on March 20.

"If the information law is adopted by the Serbian parliament without dialogue with opposition parties, this means the authorities are rejecting a round table and the recommendations of the OSCE commission," Zajedno spokesman Ivan Kovacevic told a news conference.
Another Zajedno spokesman, Slobodan Vuksanovic, described the law as "very bad, restrictive and discriminatory for private ownership".
Independent Belgrade Dnevni Telegraf in bold frontpage headlines called the law "A halter around the neck of private media".
